articles.title: In silico conservation and HLA-binding profiles of HMPV F and G protein epitopes: implications for universal vaccine development.
articles.summary: PMID: 42914659. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129282. BackgroundHuman metapneumovirus (HMPV) is a significant cause of respiratory infection, yet no licensed vaccine exists. Variability across viral subgroups, particularly in the attachment (G) protein, can complicate universal design. We assessed the immunogenetic regions in the fusion (F) and G proteins to identify stable vaccine targets.MethodsWe analyzed N = 324 Pittsburgh and N = 655 global HMPV genomes (2017-2022) for genome diversity per viral subgroup. Previously identified epitope sequences were obtained from the Immune Epitope DataBase (IEDB) for F and G proteins and sequence similarity was determined. Using NetMHCpan-4.1, we identified and computed inferred human leukocyte antigen (HLA) binding affinities for 15 epitope variants (1 or 2 substitutions) against universally common human alleles.ResultsThe F protein was highly conserved across all subgroups (>96% amino acid sequence identity). In the G protein, we identified a conserved epitope cluster (G3-G7) where epitope G7 was present in 91% of A2 genomes. Functional modeling of the G-protein epitope variants revealed that the majority of HLA alleles maintained or gained binding affinity, a subset exhibited diminished binding (escape), suggesting these regions are subject to ongoing antigenic drift. B-genotypes showed fewer retained binders and were notably underrepresented in the current epitope databases.ConclusionThe conserved F protein remains an optimal target for neutralization, while the G3-G7 cluster provides a robust secondary target for T-cell mediated immunity. A bivalent vaccine strategy could pair the stable F protein with these high-frequency G-protein epitopes to elicit an immune response. This approach addresses the A2 subgroup, and incorporating B-genotypes through ongoing surveillance and epitope mapping will be essential to achieve comprehensive, multi-antigen coverage across circulating HMPV strains.

articles.title: Differences between Canadian parents' attitudes toward routine, influenza, and COVID-19 vaccines for their children, and changes in vaccine hesitancy since the pandemic: A national cross-sectional comparative study.
articles.summary: PMID: 42962460. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129300. BackgroundEvidence suggests the COVID-19 pandemic had heterogeneous and vaccine-specific effects on parental attitudes toward childhood vaccination. A decline in vaccine confidence has been noted in some settings, however even studies reporting stable or increased confidence suggest polarized attitudes with stronger pro- and anti-vaccine views emerging concurrently. We explored differences between Canadian parents' attitudes toward childhood routine, influenza, and COVID-19 vaccination, and changes in attitudes since the pandemic.MethodsIn 2025 we conducted a cross-sectional national online survey of parents with children aged 0-17 years using a polling firm. Previously validated questions asked about parents' attitudes toward vaccination using the '5C' scale, capturing separate responses for routine, influenza, and COVID-19 vaccines. We assessed changes in attitudes about routine vaccination over time by comparing 5C responses from two previous surveys conducted in 2020 and 2021. We calculated proportions and 95% confidence intervals (CIs).ResultsRespondents (N = 1327) were proportionally representative across provinces, but not the territories. Parents were most confident in the safety of routine vaccines (71.0%, 95%CI 66.5-75.7), compared to influenza (63.7%, 95%CI 59.5-68.1) and COVID-19 (57.9%, 95%CI 53.9-62.1). The majority indicated the pandemic did not change attitudes about routine (60.8%) or influenza (63.7%) vaccination, while more than one-quarter (31.6% and 27.8%) reported that routine and influenza vaccines were more important following the pandemic. In 2025, a slightly higher proportion of parents reported low confidence in the safety and effectiveness of routine vaccines (12.7% and 9.2%, respectively), compared to 2021 (8.5% and 5.6%), and 2020 (12.2% and 6.8%).ConclusionsParental attitudes toward childhood COVID-19 vaccination differed from attitudes toward routine and influenza. Most parents reported positive or neutral impact of the pandemic on perceived importance of routine and influenza vaccines. Parents reported the highest positive attitudes toward routine vaccination mid-pandemic (2021), and parents' attitudes in 2025 were slightly less positive than in 2020 and 2021.

articles.title: Hospital-based surveillance of vaccine-preventable diseases in children: a retrospective study in a Dutch tertiary hospital (2024-2025).
articles.summary: PMID: 42925772. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129187. BackgroundVaccine-preventable diseases (VPDs) are a major cause of morbidity in children, despite established immunization programs. Surveillance of VPDs is essential to inform public health strategies and strengthen national immunization programs. This pilot study evaluated the feasibility of using routinely collected hospital data for in-hospital surveillance of pediatric VPDs.MethodsWe performed a retrospective cohort study at a tertiary hospital in the Netherlands from July 2024 to June 2025, before national implementation of RSV immunization. Children <18 years admitted with laboratory-confirmed infections caused by pathogens with available licensed vaccines were included, regardless of inclusion in the national immunization program. Feasibility was assessed based on case ascertainment, completeness of key variables and availability of vaccination information.ResultsWe included 99 children (103 VPD episodes; median age 0.6 years), of whom 60% (n = 59) required pediatric intensive care. Most hospitalizations were caused by respiratory infections, particularly RSV (n = 52) and influenza (n = 27). Case ascertainment required integration of multiple data sources, as 45% of children were tested outside the study hospital. Clinical variables were largely complete and vaccination status could be determined for 84% of episodes. Overall, 9% (n = 9) of VPD episodes occurred in fully vaccinated children. Most VPD episodes (76%; n = 78) occurred in children not vaccinated against the specific pathogen, mainly because they were too young or because the pathogen or serotype was not covered by the national immunization program or current guidelines.ConclusionsRetrospective hospital-based surveillance of pediatric VPDs is feasible and provides key information to guide efforts to optimize the national immunization program. By capturing disease severity and vaccine preventability, it complements existing surveillance data in the Netherlands.

articles.title: Childhood vaccination timeliness, under-immunization-for-age and measles effective immunity in Peru: a province and birth-cohort analysis of national survey data, 2004-2025.
articles.summary: PMID: 42945700. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129286. BackgroundUsing the survey rounds 2004-2025 of Peru's Demographic and Family Health Survey (ENDES) for children aged 12-35 months, we estimated the timeliness of sentinel vaccine doses; under-immunization-for-age and late receipt by province and birth cohort; and the gap between the proportion of children effectively immune to measles and the herd-immunity threshold.MethodsPooled cross-sections were analysed. Timeliness was measured in days, within World Health Organization age bands, among children whose vaccination card was seen; weighting and bounds addressed selection. We estimated the share of the maternal-education gap in timeliness running through antenatal and delivery care and fitted Bayesian small-area models for 196 provinces.ResultsAmong card-seen children, on-time receipt was 86.8% for bacille Calmette-Guérin (BCG), 65.3% for the third dose of diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis (DTP)-containing vaccine (DTP3), 61.1% for the first measles-containing dose and, in survey rounds 2015-2025, 39.2% for the second. For all children in the age band, recall-based bounds put DTP3 timeliness at 54.5%-63.5%, below the card-seen estimate. Children of more educated mothers had a 6.7-point lower risk of DTP3 not on time; under stated assumptions, antenatal care and institutional delivery explained 0.85 points (13%) of this gap. In the 2020-2025 birth cohort, 28 provinces were classed worse than the national level for DTP3 not on time. In the 2020-2024 birth cohort, the province-average proportion of children effectively immune to measles was 89.8%, below the herd-immunity thresholds for a basic reproduction number (R0) of 15-18; for R0 = 12, the average probability that a province fell below the threshold was 59.9%.ConclusionsMany card-seen children were vaccinated late, and card-based estimates probably overstate DTP3 timeliness. Under the assumed vaccine effectiveness and R0 of 15-18, measles immunity stayed below herd-immunity thresholds.

articles.title: Exploring perceptions of 4CMenB vaccination for gonorrhoea prevention among gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men and healthcare professionals in England: a qualitative focus group study.
articles.summary: PMID: 42962461. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129232. BackgroundIn November 2023, the Joint Committee on Vaccination and Immunisation advised the UK government to introduce a targeted, opportunistic vaccination programme using 4CMenB in sexual health services to prevent gonorrhoea primarily in gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men (GBMSM) at higher risk of infection. Evidence on4CMenB vaccination acceptability was required.MethodsThree focus group discussions (FGDs) were conducted with 17 GBMSM aged ≥18 years, resident in England, who self-reported bacterial sexually transmitted infection or ≥ 5 sexual partners in the previous 12-months, alongside one FGD with five sexual healthcare professionals (HCPs). Data were analysed using thematic analysis and organised and interpreted using the Vaccine Uptake Continuum and the Social Ecological Model.ResultsParticipating GBMSM and HCPs generally expressed positive perceptions of 4CMenB vaccination. GBMSM described vaccination as supporting sexual wellbeing and reducing anxiety about gonorrhoea. While the estimated effectiveness (30-35%) was perceived as modest, it did not deter acceptability but reduced willingness to actively seek vaccination. Structural constraints (e.g. limited appointment availability) and restrictive eligibility criteria were identified as barriers to equitable uptake. Community-based delivery models were supported as a potential approach to improve access. HCPs drew on mpox vaccination experience to anticipate implementation challenges and emphasised clear guidance and sustainable resourcing. Additional protection against meningitis was generally a secondary influence.Conclusions4CMenB vaccination for gonorrhoea was acceptable to participating GBMSM and HCPs; however, uptake is likely to depend on ease of access, clear communication, and system-level support. Addressing structural constraints and supporting community-based delivery may help achieve equitable delivery of 4CMenB.

articles.title: End-of-season influenza vaccine effectiveness against a(H3N2) and B/Victoria in Beijing, China, 2025/26 season.
articles.summary: PMID: 42950746. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129273. IntroductionThis study aimed to estimate the end-of-season influenza vaccine effectiveness (VE) against A(H3N2) and B/Victoria in the 2025/26 season in Beijing, China.MethodsWe used a test-negative design to assess influenza VE among outpatients with influenza-like illness (ILI) enrolled through the Beijing influenza sentinel virological surveillance system from September 2025 (week 40/2025) to May 2026 (week 21/2026). Cases were ILI patients who tested positive for influenza; controls were those who tested negative. The VE was estimated using non-conditional multiple logistic regression models, adjusting for age (modelled as a natural cubic spline), sex, presence of comorbidities, area of residence, and calendar week (modelled as a natural cubic spline).ResultsAmong 20,749 ILI patients tested, 4875 (23.5%) were positive for influenza, with A(H3N2) and B/Victoria being the predominant strains. Adjusted VE was 26.4% (95% CI: 17.8 to 34.1) against any influenza, 22.2% (95% CI: 11.3 to 31.7) against A(H3N2), and 34.7% (95% CI: 19.6 to 47.0) against B/Victoria, with the highest VE observed in adults aged 18-59 years (53.0%, 95%CI: 37.0 to 64.9) against any influenza. The adjusted VE was similar for those vaccinated in 2025/26 only (38.7%, 95%CI: 15.6 to 55.5) or both 2024/25 and 2025/26 seasons (35.1%, 95%CI: 16.5 to 49.6), but higher than those vaccinated in 2024/25 only (17.0%, 95%CI: -16.1 to 40.7) among B/Victoria. For A(H3N2), the VE point estimate was higher among those vaccinated in the 2025/26 season only (27.9%, 95%CI: 11.5 to 41.2) than among those vaccinated in both seasons (17.9%, 95%CI: 4.0 to 29.7) and 2024/25 only (-6.1%, 95%CI: -28.7 to 12.5).ConclusionOur findings indicate that seasonal vaccination reduced laboratory-confirmed influenza among outpatients by approximately a quarter, with higher VE in adults aged 18-59 years. VE estimates according to vaccination status over two consecutive seasons showed different patterns for A(H3N2) and B/Victoria. These real-world findings support the ongoing public health value of influenza vaccination and highlight the importance of continuous virological surveillance, prevention, and control policy.

articles.title: Monitoring of adverse events following 2024-2025 BNT162b2 KP.2 COVID-19 vaccination in the United States.
articles.summary: PMID: 42933241. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129296. Large real-world data studies are needed to understand the safety profile of the 2024-2025 adapted COVID-19 vaccines. This study monitors the occurrence of 20 adverse events of special interest (AESIs) following 2024-2025 BNT162b2 KP.2 COVID-19 vaccination. Individuals age ≥ 6 months vaccinated between 08/22/2024 and 03/10/2025 were identified within the Optum pre-adjudicated database. A self-controlled risk interval design was used to compare the incidence of 20 AESIs during a risk period following vaccination to a subsequent control period among 894,852,024-2025 BNT162b2 COVID-19-vaccinated individuals (median age: 46.9 years). While point estimates were higher in the risk period compared to the control period for non-febrile convulsions/seizures (relative incidence: 1.29; 95% CI: 0.92-1.81) and herpes zoster (relative incidence: 1.05; 95% CI: 0.59-1.85), the magnitude was not significant. No safety signals were identified following 2024-2025 BNT162b2 COVID-19 vaccination among commercially insured individuals in the United States, though the study was underpowered for rare outcomes.

articles.title: Ischemic stroke after bivalent mRNA COVID-19 vaccination and influenza vaccination during the 2022-2023 season: a multi-site self-controlled case series study.
articles.summary: PMID: 42914658. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129263. BackgroundThe Vaccine Safety Datalink (VSD) detected a statistical signal for ischemic events (ischemic stroke or transient ischemic attack) following bivalent mRNA COVID-19 vaccination through prospective surveillance during 2022-2023. Although multiple studies from other surveillance systems and countries reported no increased risk, important methodological limitations remained. This U.S. study addressed those limitations by evaluating the ischemic stroke risk following bivalent mRNA COVID-19 vaccination, influenza vaccination, and their same-day coadministration using an event-dependent self-controlled case series (SCCS) design.MethodsStudy outcomes included first-ever ischemic stroke (primary outcome), first-in-1-year ischemic stroke (secondary outcome), and ischemic events (exploratory outcomes), identified using ICD-10-CM codes in inpatient and emergency department settings during September 1, 2022-March 31, 2023, among individuals aged ≥12 years across eight VSD sites. Analyses were conducted separately for Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna bivalent vaccines, with relative incidences (RI) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) estimated for 1-21-day and 1-42-day risk intervals, using person-time outside these intervals as the control period. Subgroup analyses were performed by age group (12-64, ≥65 years) and history of documented SARS-CoV-2 infection.ResultsA total of 6510 first-ever ischemic strokes were identified among more than 6.8 million participants. Among recipients of Pfizer-BioNTech bivalent COVID-19 and influenza vaccines, no statistically significant increased risk of first-ever ischemic stroke was observed following bivalent COVID-19 vaccination (RI = 0.94; 95% CI: 0.63-1.41), influenza vaccination (RI = 0.95; 95% CI: 0.82-1.10), or same-day coadministration (RI = 1.15; 95% CI: 0.88-1.49) within 1-21-day risk intervals; findings were similar for 1-42-day intervals. Comparable null results were observed for Moderna vaccine and across all subgroups, secondary, and exploratory outcomes.ConclusionNo increased risk of ischemic stroke was found following bivalent mRNA COVID-19 vaccination, influenza vaccination, or their coadministration in this multi-site SCCS study. These findings are consistent with previous studies and underscore the importance of continued vaccine safety monitoring.

articles.title: Faster waning of immunity to influenza vaccine strains reintroduced into subsequent seasons: A human cohort study.
articles.summary: PMID: 42945703. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129258. BackgroundSeasonal influenza vaccines are updated annually, and some seasons reuse strains from prior formulations. Although repeated vaccination has been associated with lower-than-expected post-vaccination titers, whether it alters immune durability remains unclear. We compared strain-specific waning rates across seasons in which vaccine formulations shared one or more strains.MethodsWe analyzed hemagglutination inhibition (HAI) titers from a longitudinal vaccine cohort (2016-2023). For strains reused across seasons, we compared waning rate from season i to i + 1 (initial waning period) with waning from i + 1 to i + 2 (second waning period). Mixed-effects models estimated differences in strain-specific waning between periods, adjusting for age, BMI, previous vaccination in season i - 1, and other covariates.ResultsSeven vaccine strains were reused across seasons (768 strain-specific measurements from 275 participants). The B lineage strain Phu/13 appeared in all seasons. Across repeatedly used subtype A and lineage B viruses, antibody levels waned significantly faster after subsequent vaccination. Among adults, the average increase in waning rate during the second period was 0.011 (H1N1), 0.108 (H3N2), 0.056 (Yamagata), and 0.049 (Victoria) log2 titer per month. Age modified these relationships, with slower waning in older adults for H1N1 and in teenagers for Yamagata. Waning also varied by strains, with BR08 waning faster than WA19. Higher pre-vaccination titers were associated with slower waning for H1N1 and H3N2, whereas larger post-vaccination boosts predicted faster waning for all virus strains.ConclusionsWe found that the waning rates of certain vaccine strains may differ between initial and subsequent waning periods. Further investigation is warranted to optimize annual influenza vaccine composition updates.

articles.title: Brazilian version of the Vaccine Trust Gauge for adolescents.
articles.summary: PMID: 42925770. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129270. AimTo cross-culturally adapt the Vaccine Trust Gauge (VTG) for the Brazilian context and evaluate its content validity, structural validity, internal consistency, and test-retest reliability among adolescents.MethodsThis methodological study involved the cross-cultural adaptation of the VTG and the evaluation of its content validity, structural validity, internal consistency, and test-retest reliability. Content validity was assessed by an expert committee. Pre-testing was conducted with adolescents to evaluate clarity and acceptability. Internal structure was examined using confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) with the weighted least squares mean and variance adjusted estimator for ordinal data. Reliability was assessed using McDonald's omega and test-retest analysis with the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC).ResultsThe Brazilian version demonstrated strong content validity (Content Validity Index = 0.90). Pre-testing indicated good comprehension following minor linguistic adjustments. CFA supported the three-factor model (trust, importance, recommendation), with excellent fit indices (CFI = 0.972; TLI = 0.962; RMSEA = 0.056; SRMR = 0.052). Internal consistency ranged from 0.70 to 0.89. Test-retest analysis showed moderate temporal stability (ICC = 0.74).ConclusionThe Brazilian VTG provides initial evidence of validity and reliability for assessing vaccine trust among adolescents. The instrument may support monitoring of vaccine trust, inform targeted interventions, and guide public health strategies across diverse immunization contexts.

articles.title: A qualitative examination of factors impacting Black and Latino sexual minority men's vaccination decision-making and experiences: application of the stages of vaccine readiness and action theoretical framework.
articles.summary: PMID: 42962463. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129283. BackgroundBlack and Latino sexual minority men (BLSMM) experience persistent inequities in vaccine uptake, driven by structural barriers, medical mistrust, misinformation, and limited culturally responsive communication. This study applied the Stages of Vaccine Readiness and Action (SVRA) framework to examine vaccine decision-making among BLSMM during infectious disease outbreaks in the United States.MethodsWe conducted a qualitative interpretative phenomenological study using semi-structured interviews with 41 BLSMM in California and New York between August 2021 and December 2022. Interviews explored vaccine experiences and barriers and facilitators to uptake. Data were analyzed using thematic content analysis guided by the SVRA framework.ResultsParticipants ranged from 19 to 65 years; 73% identified as Black and 93% as male. Vaccine decision-making was dynamic and shaped by individual and structural factors across five SVRA stages: skepticism, curiosity, readiness, action, and maintenance. Skepticism reflected medical mistrust, misinformation, safety concerns, and distrust of governmental and scientific institutions. Curiosity centered on vaccine development, side effects, and conflicting information. Readiness and action were facilitated by trusted healthcare providers, protecting oneself and others, chronic health conditions, and community-based vaccination. Transportation, appointment systems, employment demands, and healthcare access impeded vaccination. Maintenance was undermined by vaccine fatigue, booster burden, side-effect concerns, and changing perceptions of vaccine effectiveness.ConclusionVaccine decision-making among BLSMM occurs along a continuum shaped by psychosocial and structural determinants. Findings support culturally responsive education, trust-building, community-engaged interventions, and structural supports. Similar barriers may affect uptake and sustained engagement with long-acting injectable HIV prevention and treatment modalities.

articles.title: Exposure to natural disasters and vaccination indicators: a systematic review and directions for future research.
articles.summary: PMID: 42945701. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129277. Global routine childhood immunization has stagnated for almost two decades, leaving children vulnerable to both immediate and long-term health risks from infectious diseases. Identifying and mitigating impediments to childhood vaccination, such as barriers resulting from exposure to natural disasters, is vital for maintaining population health. While there is general understanding that disasters have the potential to disrupt vaccination services, well designed studies on the degree to which exposure to natural disasters affects vaccination indicators are limited. Understanding the effects of natural disasters on vaccine preventable diseases is an important area for future research as some natural disasters are becoming more frequent and intense due to climate change. To understand the current state of research on exposure to natural disasters and vaccination indicators (i.e., vaccination metrics including administration, coverage, rates), we conducted a systematic literature review of all literature in Embase, Google Scholar, PubMed, and Web of Science up until September 11-12, 2025. We aimed to identify relevant peer reviewed literature focusing on natural disasters and immunization and to assess them for relevance and inclusion. Seventeen studies met the criteria for inclusion. These studies examined the relationship between exposure to cyclones/hurricanes, droughts, earthquakes, flooding, heat waves, and multiple disaster types and changes in vaccination among different age groups. Most (16/17 (94.12%)) papers identified a connection or association between exposure to natural disasters and reduced vaccination indicators. The majority (13/17 (76.47%)) of studies focused on early-childhood vaccinations. Characteristics that affect vulnerability to under-vaccination-exposure level, geographical location, socioeconomic status-were assessed in several papers. Areas for future research include quantifying the degree to which different disaster types affect multiple vaccination indicators within the same individuals and changes in communities over time.

articles.title: Boosting hybrid immunity with intranasal live-attenuated or intramuscular mRNA vaccination prevents SARS-CoV-2 XBB.1.5 transmission.
articles.summary: PMID: 42950580. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129298. Rapid antigenic evolution of SARS-CoV-2 and waning immunity have reduced antibody-mediated neutralization, enabling breakthrough infections and sustained transmission despite widespread immunity. This highlights the need for variant-adapted booster vaccines. However, pre-existing immunity may influence the magnitude and specificity of immune responses induced by variant-adapted booster vaccination. Using the Syrian hamster model, we previously described a safe and efficient mucosal vaccination approach using live attenuated viruses (LAV) based on a "One-to-Stop (OTS)" codon modification strategy. Whether OTS vaccines are suitable as effective booster vaccines in the presence of pre-existing mucosal immunity remained unaddressed. Here, we modeled pre-existing hybrid immunity in Syrian hamsters using intramuscular bivalent mRNA vaccination followed by SARS-CoV-2 infection and subsequently administered heterologous intranasal OTS-LAV or intramuscular mRNA XBB.1.5 booster vaccination. Both booster strategies significantly increased XBB.1.5-binding- and neutralizing antibodies systemically and at mucosal sites. In contrast, booster vaccination left SARS-CoV-2 specific T cell frequencies unchanged. While all hybrid-immune animals were protected from disease following XBB.1.5 challenge infection, virus transmission was completely blocked only after booster vaccination and was associated with the absence of infectious virus in nasal samples. Collectively, using OTS-LAV we provide a proof of concept that intranasal LAV vaccination can effectively boost pre-existing hybrid immunity and restrict viral transmission. These findings support the use of OTS-LAV as a heterologous booster strategy against SARS-CoV-2 and demonstrate that variant-adapted booster vaccination can efficiently limit transmission, a strategy highly desired for tackling emerging respiratory infections.

articles.title: mRNA vaccine encoding multimerized AIV-M2e fused to MHC-II invariant chain motif and Pan-DR epitope confers protection against H9N2 virus in chickens.
articles.summary: PMID: 42933243. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129280. Avian influenza viruses (AIVs) remain a major threat to global poultry health and production. The risk of cross-species transmission among diverse AIV subtypes poses a significant challenge to disease control, underscoring the need for vaccines that provide broad and durable protection. However, existing inactivated and vector-based vaccines provide limited cross-subtype coverage and durable immunity against antigenically diverse AIVs. In contrast, the success of mRNA vaccines against SARS-CoV-2 has accelerated vaccine development by enabling rapid, flexible, and scalable vaccine design compared with conventional platforms. We designed an mRNA vaccine encoding four tandem repeats of the conserved influenza M2 ectodomain (4xM2e), fused to the chicken invariant chain (Ii) motif and a 13-amino-acid universal Pan-DR-binding epitope (PADRE). We hypothesized that this design would enhance anti-M2e antibody responses while promoting efficient antigen processing and CD4+ T-helper cell activation, thereby inducing systemic and mucosal immunity against AIV infection in chickens. The mRNA construct was delivered via standard lipid nanoparticles (LNPs), and vaccine efficacy was evaluated following intramuscular (IM) and intranasal (IN) administration. Our data demonstrated a modest increase in systemic and mucosal antibody responses, accompanied by enhanced T-cell proliferation and increased CD4+ and γδ+ T-cell populations. Following challenge with A/turkey/Wisconsin/1/1966/H9N2 virus, vaccinated birds exhibited significantly reduced viral shedding regardless of the route of administration. Histopathological analysis further demonstrated largely preserved pulmonary architecture with minimal inflammation, demonstrating effective maintenance of mucosal barrier integrity. To assess the cross-protective potential and functional activity of anti-M2e antibodies, we demonstrated in vitro heterosubtypic recognition of PR8/H1N1 and confirmed their functional relevance by antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC). Together, our findings demonstrate that the present mRNA vaccine construct, encoding a structurally optimized multimerized M2e protein fused to PADRE and the Ii motif, represents a safe and effective vaccine strategy with the potential to confer broad protective immunity against AIV infection in chickens.

articles.title: Maternal history of child marriage, educational attainment, and children's vaccination: Evidence from the Indonesian Demographic and Health Survey, 2017.
articles.summary: PMID: 42962462. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129271. IntroductionChild marriage, i.e., first cohabitating before 18 years of age, is a critical social issue that could affect a women's educational attainment, their own health, and their child's health. This study investigated the association between maternal history of child marriage and childhood vaccination rates in Indonesia, and analyzed whether maternal education was an effect modifier of this relationship.MethodsThis study analyzed the 2017 Indonesian Demographic and Health Survey, a nationally representative cross-sectional survey. Maternal history of child marriage was assessed as the main exposure, full childhood vaccination as the outcome, and maternal completion of high school as the potential effect modifier. Robust Poisson regression was used to examine the association between maternal history of child marriage and full childhood vaccination, adjusted for maternal, paternal, household, and child-related factors.ResultsOverall, among 7785 mothers, 22.1% had a history of child marriage, and 64.9% of children were fully vaccinated. Full vaccination was 56.1% among mothers with a history of child marriage, compared to 67.4% among mothers without. In an adjusted model, mothers with a history of child marriage had 0.86 (95% CI: 0.81, 0.91) times the prevalence of fully vaccinating their children compared to mothers without this history. There was a non-significant trend (P = 0.253) between maternal education and history of child marriage, with vaccination highest in those with no child marriage and a high school education (71.3%), and lowest in those with a history of child marriage and no high school education (54.8%).ConclusionsMothers with a history of child marriage are more likely to not vaccinate their children. This study emphasizes a critical need for public health and socioeconomic interventions to prevent child marriage and increase children's vaccination rates in households whose mothers have had a history of child marriage.

articles.title: Hemagglutinin- and neuraminidase-targeting antibody responses after receipt of egg-based inactivated or recombinant influenza vaccines among adults aged 18-64 years.
articles.summary: PMID: 42945702. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129281. IntroductionAntibodies to hemagglutinin (HA) and neuraminidase (NA) are independent surrogates of protection from influenza yet only HA content is standardized in vaccines. Egg-based inactivated influenza vaccines (IIV) contain HA and NA from egg-adapted viruses. Recombinant influenza vaccines (RIV) solely include HA without egg-adapted modifications. Humoral responses to both HA and NA can provide valuable insights into vaccine effectiveness.MethodsIn a randomized trial comparing 2022-2023 quadrivalent RIV and standard dose (SD) IIV among adults aged 18-64 years, a subgroup of participants had sera collected pre-vaccination, 1-, and 6-months post-vaccination. Neutralization titers were determined for both cell- and egg-based vaccine reference viruses and representative circulating viruses using single cycle replication-based IRINA. NA-inhibiting responses to N1 and N2 were evaluated using ELLA; ELISA was used to measure N2-binding response.ResultsAnti-HA responses to cell-based type A and B/Yamagata viruses were two-fold higher among RIV versus SD-IIV recipients; the difference in response to cell-based B/Victoria virus was not statistically significant. Compared to responses to cell-based vaccine viruses, post-vaccination sera reacted comparably to circulating viruses, except to A(H1N1)pdm09 (2-6-fold reduction). Compared to HI antibodies, neutralizing antibodies waned faster to most vaccine viruses. SD-IIV recipients showed no rise in NA-inhibiting antibodies to mammalian cell-grown viruses. Conversely, there was a ≥ 4-fold rise in ELLA GMTs to N1 (13%) and N2 (37%) antigens that were prepared in eggs, despite no changes in NA sequences. Baseline egg/cell titer ratios were 1.3 for N1 and 4.2 for N2 antigens, and they increased by approximately 2-fold after vaccination in SD-IIV but not RIV recipients.ConclusionHA-targeting antibody responses were more robust in RIV-recipients. SD-IIV did not elicit meaningful NA-inhibiting antibody responses to viruses grown in mammalian cells but did boost antibodies to egg-grown viruses. Sourcing NA antigens from cell-grown viruses should be considered when assessing humoral responses to vaccination.
